topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: A C++ expression is not executed directly by the processor as source text. The compiler and runtime turn it into machine operations, while the operating system controls access to protected resources. This chapter separates those layers. We will compute a small result in ordinary C++, query process information through POSIX interfaces, and observe the distinction between a library call and the system boundary it may use.

topics.title: 1.1.1 Understanding Instructions and Registers
topics.summary: A processor executes instructions defined by its instruction-set architecture. Registers hold operands, addresses, and intermediate state close to execution units. A compiler maps C++ expressions to those instructions under the language’s observable-behavior rules; one source operation may become several instructions, be folded into another, or disappear when its result is unnecessary.

blocks.text: An instruction-set architecture defines the instructions software can use. A microarchitecture is an implementation of that architecture: the execution units, queues, caches, prediction machinery, and other mechanisms that carry those instructions out. Two processors can run the same executable while taking different amounts of time. Conversely, two executables built from the same C++ can use different instructions because the compiler was given different target options. This distinction explains why “it is x86-64” is not a complete performance description.

blocks.text: Registers are not an extra addressable array that ordinary portable C++ can freely inspect. The compiler decides how to keep intermediate values, and the calling convention assigns roles to some machine state across function calls. A debugger may show a source variable as optimized out when there is no recoverable independent location for it. That does not mean the variable was forgotten; its contribution may already be represented in another value.

It also leaves room for the source program to remain correct when the implementation changes.

topics.title: 1.1.2 Understanding the Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle
topics.summary: Fetch, decode, and execute provide a useful conceptual model for instruction processing. Modern processors may pipeline stages, execute multiple operations, predict branches, and reorder internal work while preserving the architecture’s required externally visible behavior. A simple serial cycle diagram is therefore a teaching abstraction rather than a literal timing schedule for every instruction.

blocks.text: The compiler also reorders and transforms work when permitted. Performance reasoning must consider both compiler transformations and hardware execution. Correct synchronization and defined behavior constrain what transformations are allowed; volatile is not a general way to freeze an entire computation or make shared-memory code safe.
rich: The compiler also reorders and transforms work when permitted. Performance reasoning must consider both compiler transformations and hardware execution. Correct synchronization and defined behavior constrain what transformations are allowed; volatile is not a general way to freeze an entire computation or make shared-memory code safe.

blocks.text: The fetch-decode-execute model describes a dependency: instructions must be obtained, interpreted, and carried out. It does not require every instruction to complete all three stages before the next one begins. A pipeline overlaps stages for different instructions. Multiple execution units can perform independent operations, and speculative work can begin before a branch is resolved. A simple diagram deliberately suppresses those details to make the basic flow understandable.

blocks.text: Data dependencies constrain that freedom. If one operation needs the result of another, the second cannot produce its correct result until the relevant value is available. Independent operations may offer more overlap. In a sum, each update to one accumulator depends on the preceding update; an optimizer can sometimes change the evaluation structure when the language permits the resulting arithmetic behavior. Integer overflow and floating-point reassociation rules matter here. A mathematically equivalent arrangement is not automatically an equivalent C++ program.

blocks.text: Separate instruction latency from throughput. Latency concerns how long a dependent result takes to become available. Throughput concerns how much work can complete over an interval when enough independent work exists. A system may have good throughput while an individual request experiences substantial delay. Later server chapters distinguish the same two ideas at application scale: requests per second and per-request latency answer different questions.

blocks.text: Branches introduce another source of variation. A processor can predict a direction and start useful work, but an incorrect prediction may require discarding speculative results. This does not give the program permission to violate its language-level behavior. It does mean that two inputs following different branch patterns can have different runtime costs even when their source-level loop counts are equal. Do not turn a count of C++ statements into an unsupported cycle estimate.

blocks.text: For a beginner’s experiment, inspect rather than tune. Build a small function with debug information at both -O0 and -O2, then compare its instructions. Observe whether a loop remains, whether a constant appears, and whether the call itself survives. Keep the input/output contract unchanged. The purpose is to learn that the compiler and processor both contribute to execution, not to decide that one optimization level is universally better for debugging, latency, or every workload. (GCC, CLANG)

topics.title: 1.2.1 Distinguishing User and Kernel Space
topics.summary: Ordinary application code runs with user-mode privileges in a process address space. Kernel code manages protected operations such as scheduling, virtual memory, and device access. This separation is a protection mechanism, not simply a naming convention for folders or libraries. A process cannot legitimately access arbitrary kernel memory merely by forming a pointer value.

blocks.text: System calls provide controlled entry points for requested operations. The kernel validates arguments and permissions and reports results through the platform’s interface. A failure can reflect invalid input, resource limits, permissions, or changing external state. Systems code must treat those failures as part of normal operation rather than assume a valid C++ call expression guarantees success.

blocks.text: A process address space gives a program a view of memory. It is not a promise that every numerically representable address refers to memory the program owns. A pointer value can be formed incorrectly, refer to an expired object, or identify a page without the required permission. The operating system’s page protections and C++’s object rules are different boundaries. Passing a page-permission check does not establish a valid object lifetime or a legal typed access.

blocks.text: User mode and kernel mode describe privilege levels of execution, not the identity of the human running a command. A program started by the root account still executes ordinary application instructions in user mode and reaches privileged services through controlled interfaces. Elevated credentials can change whether a request is authorized; they do not convert every pointer dereference into a legitimate kernel-memory access.

blocks.text: The boundary also affects error interpretation. A failed open can mean that a path does not exist, access is denied, a descriptor limit was reached, or some other condition described by the native interface occurred. The C++ expression can be well-formed while the operating-system operation fails. This is why the book treats native errors as expected states to model, not merely as exceptional mistakes by the programmer. (OPEN)

blocks.text: Think of a file descriptor as a process-local reference to a resource managed through the kernel. It is not the file’s complete contents, a globally meaningful identifier, or a permanent serial number. Descriptor 5 in one process need not refer to the same resource as descriptor 5 in another. Even within one process, the number can be reused after release. The resource-wrapper chapters turn that observation into an ownership discipline.

blocks.text: Use the least privileged environment that can perform the lesson. The supplied examples do not need root, raw device access, or changes to kernel policy. A permission failure is a reason to inspect the requirement and environment before adding privilege. Do not reinterpret a denied facility as a language defect or silently disable a protection mechanism just to make a test appear successful.

A program started by the root account still executes ordinary application instructions in user mode and reaches privileged services through controlled interfaces. Elevated credentials can change whether a request is authorized; they do not convert every pointer dereference into a legitimate kernel-memory access.

The boundary also affects error interpretation. A failed open can mean that a path does not exist, access is denied, a descriptor limit was reached, or some other condition described by the native interface occurred. The C++ expression can be well-formed while the operating-system operation fails. This is why the book treats native errors as expected states to model, not merely as exceptional mistakes by the programmer. (OPEN)

Think of a file descriptor as a process-local reference to a resource managed through the kernel. It is not the file’s complete contents, a globally meaningful identifier, or a permanent serial number. Descriptor 5 in one process need not refer to the same resource as descriptor 5 in another. Even within one process, the number can be reused after release. The resource-wrapper chapters turn that observation into an ownership discipline.

Use the least privileged environment that can perform the lesson. The supplied examples do not need root, raw device access, or changes to kernel policy. A permission failure is a reason to inspect the requirement and environment before adding privilege. If a container restricts process tracing or socket creation, record that boundary and run the relevant lab in an ordinary development VM. Do not reinterpret a denied facility as a language defect or silently disable a protection mechanism just to make a test appear successful.

blocks.text: Walk a hypothetical five-byte output through three native results: two bytes, one byte, and two bytes. After the first call, the next operation must start at offset two and request three bytes. After the second, it must start at offset three and request two. Save the error at the failing boundary before performing other operations that might change it.

paragraphs: Make a directory containing only this chapter’s source and the supplied check header. Compile with explicit C++20 mode, warnings, and debug information. Run the executable, capture its return status, and redirect its output to a disposable file. Compare that file with the exact expected bytes. This establishes a functional baseline before introducing diagnostic tools.

Next compile at a different optimization level into a differently named output. Inspect the sum in the generated assembly. Write a short explanation of what changed and what remained required by the source. An acceptable explanation can say that no separate loop remains; it cannot conclude that “the CPU did not execute the program” because an optimizer removed an unnecessary runtime calculation.

code: // The integer is converted to uint64_t.

overview.explanation: Arrows show value and execution flow. This is a source-level trace, not a claim about a particular CPU instruction sequence.

focus.title: Separate the interface from the expression
explain: std::uint64_t is an unsigned integer type with exactly 64 value bits on platforms that provide it. The parameter x is a value copy.
Parentheses compute x+5 first; multiplication then produces the result. return passes that value to the caller.
The closing brace ends the function body.
focus.what: The function maps one unsigned input value to one unsigned output value.
focus.where: Its declaration and body are visible to the compiler before main.
focus.why: A named function provides one place to inspect and change this arithmetic rule.
focus.invariant: For the fixture 7, the intermediate is 12 and the result is 48. Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2^64 if its range is exceeded.
focus.risk: Assuming these are unbounded mathematical integers gives wrong results for large inputs. The source alone does not promise one particular machine instruction sequence.

focus.title: Observe rather than assume
explain: main begins the program’s entry-point body.
The nested call completes before its result is inserted into cout. The string adds a newline.
The closing brace ends main; falling off the end is equivalent to returning zero.
focus.what: Output exposes a result that can be checked in a test.
focus.where: This is the runtime caller of transform.
focus.why: A tiny input and exact output help debug arithmetic before inspecting generated instructions.
focus.invariant: For this fixture the output is 48 followed by a newline.
focus.risk: A different integer width or changed operator order may change results; keep tests near the rule.
